Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Nigeria predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording, including visits, files, and NCD records. Recent studies confirm 100% reliance on paper files with 0% electronic records in surveyed PHCs, and national EHR adoption remains low at ~18%, with rural areas facing acute barriers like unreliable electricity (41% grid access), poor internet (40% penetration), high costs, low digital literacy (26.7% proficient workers), and lack of training. Digital systems like DHIS2 are used nationally for aggregate HMIS reporting, with some pilots for immunization logistics (e.g., ~9,000 facilities reporting stock data), but point-of-care patient records remain manual; data is collated on paper and entered at LGA/district levels. Pilots exist (e.g., offline hardware trials, state telemedicine), but are isolated/donor-driven, not scaling to majority of ~30,000 rural PHCs. Key barriers: infrastructure deficits, policy fragmentation, resistance to change from paper workflows. National ambitions (e.g., NHMIS digitalization) contrast sharply with rural reality of paper dominance, limiting point-of-service digitalisation.

revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Nigeria continue to rely almost entirely on paper-based registers for point-of-care data capture, including patient visits, files and non-communicable disease records. National electronic health record adoption remains low, at around 18%, and the digitisation programmes now underway (such as Lagos State's Primary Health Care EMR rollout, covering 100 of 326 facilities as of May 2025, and Abia State's newly announced E-Health project of February 2026) are concentrated in state capitals and urban facilities rather than rural clinics. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet access, low digital literacy among healthcare workers, and limited training and funding. Aggregate reporting systems such as DHIS2 operate at higher administrative levels, but data capture at the rural point of service remains manual.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Nigeria record criminal cases and complaints using manual paper-based systems, including handwritten statements, petitions, police reports, and exhibits logs. A 2020 assessment confirms records are kept in hard copy at stations, with limited electronic storage only at state headquarters; computer networks and databases see very low use across formations, and many cases go unrecorded due to officer fatigue.US Department of Justice report Academic studies highlight inadequate police presence and infrastructure (power, roads) in rural areas, relying on community policing without mention of digital tools at point-of-service.Heliyon study National digital initiatives exist: WAPIS (Interpol/EU-funded national criminal database since 2019), pilots like CRIMS, and planned smart stations (2025), but these are centralized or urban-focused, with no evidence of routine rural deployment.Interpol WAPIS Barriers include poor infrastructure, limited resources/training, and low government commitment to nationwide rollout. National ambitions for digital policing contrast sharply with rural paper reality, where data is likely aggregated manually upward.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Nigeria record criminal cases and complaints using entirely manual, paper-based systems: handwritten statements, petitions, police reports and exhibit logs, with only limited electronic storage at state headquarters level. As of mid-2026, the Federal Government and the Nigeria Police Trust Fund have signed a Memorandum of Understanding under Project BRIDGE to map police stations and connect them to the national fibre backbone, with associated plans for AI-assisted statement transcription and case management, but implementation is only beginning, phased over at least the next 12 months, and commentators explicitly flag the risk that rural and hard-to-reach stations will lag behind urban connectivity. Data capture at the point of service in rural stations therefore remains entirely paper-based.

revision_notes: Confirmed with updated 2026 evidence; the original UNECA CRVS snapshot PDF could not be re-fetched (timeout/access error) but its finding of predominantly manual, paper-based rural registration is corroborated by newer sources. Nigeria's e-CRVS rollout has accelerated markedly through 2025-2026: Delta State ended manual registration in March 2026, Kano recorded around 103,000 electronic registrations by March 2026, and further states are onboarding via the NPC/UNICEF Vital Registration (VitalReg) application. However, digital registration is currently limited mainly to children under five; older age groups still require manual or attestation-based processes; only NPC staff (not the public) can perform digital registration; and staff explicitly revert to paper when network connectivity fails, which is common in rural areas. A UN Stats operational readiness assessment likewise found existing registration processes 'predominantly manual and paper-based' nationally, with the VitalReg system's technical architecture 'not fit to be scaled'. This mixed but expanding picture supports 'Mostly paper - some digital' (2) rather than a majority-digital status in rural registry offices; it does not yet meet the bar for 'Mostly digital - some paper' (3).
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Nigeria are in an active but partial transition from paper to digital birth registration. The National Population Commission, with UNICEF and partners, is rolling out the electronic Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (e-CRVS) system and the Vital Registration (VitalReg) mobile application, with several states (including Delta and Kano) having ended or substantially reduced manual registration for young children during 2026. However, digital registration is currently restricted mainly to children under five, with older age groups still processed manually or via attestation, and registration remains staff-operated using Personal Digital Assistants rather than self-service. Field registrars in rural and hard-to-reach areas frequently revert to paper records when network connectivity fails, and birth registration completeness remains low overall (around 53-57% for under-fives, with certification rates near 30%), with the largest gaps in rural communities. Data capture at rural registry offices is therefore best characterised as predominantly paper-based with a growing but still partial digital component.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Nigeria predominantly use paper-based registers for recording attendance, administrative data, and learning outcomes at the point of service. For example, in Nassarawo Primary School (Adamawa State, rural northeast), teachers manually tick names in worn paper books daily, facing issues like rain damage and termite destruction; digital backups are personal copies, not systematic.DPI Africa (2026). National EMIS (NEMIS on DHIS2) exists for aggregation, with pilots like EdoEMIS (51 schools including rural, daily digital attendance via app) and training in 12 states, but these are isolated or state-specific donor projects not representing most rural facilities.DHIS2.org (2025). World Bank analysis confirms schools complete paper census forms forwarded for central digital entry, not digital at school level.World Bank EMIS Study. Barriers: poor electricity/internet (41% offline), low digital literacy (<20% rural youth computer-proficient), high costs, insecurity. National policy pushes EMIS/DPI (UBEC digital platform 2024, GenU9ja connectivity), but rural reality lags with manual processes and slow pilot scaling.

revision_notes: Confirmed. Fetched cited sources; a DPI Africa field report (published March 2026) documents a rural primary school in Adamawa State still using handwritten paper attendance registers with no systematic digital backup, describing continued paper reliance as the norm across Nigeria despite the national DPI push. The DHIS2/Data Science Nigeria EdoEMIS pilot (implemented 2023, reported May 2025) covers only 51 schools (urban and rural) in Edo State, a small, state-specific programme not yet representative of the roughly 30,000+ rural primary schools nationally. World Bank EMIS analysis confirms the standard national model is paper census forms completed at school level and digitised centrally, not digital capture at the school. Score 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Nigeria predominantly record attendance and administrative data on paper at the point of service. A March 2026 field account from Nassarawo Primary School in rural Adamawa State illustrates the norm nationally: teachers mark handwritten registers daily, with no systematic digital backup, exposing records to damage and loss. Isolated digital pilots exist, notably the DHIS2-based EdoEMIS system introduced in Edo State in 2023, which by 2025 provided real-time attendance and performance tracking for 51 schools including some rural facilities, but this remains a small, donor-supported programme rather than the national norm. The standard national practice, reflected in World Bank analysis of the Education Management Information System, is for schools to complete paper forms that are digitised at a higher administrative level rather than captured digitally at the school itself. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet access and low digital literacy among rural teachers and pupils.
